# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles geographic coordinates, administrative affiliations,
foundation chronologies and longitudinal demographic trajectories for 1.480
catalogued settlements across four maritime macro-regions in South Asia (1.316.175
km²) between 1498AD and 1757AD. The catalogued network links fortified naval
headquarters, open riverine and roadstead factory posts, textile artisan centres
and agrarian market towns into an integrated spatial hierarchy. By reconciling
contemporary company muster rolls, municipal tax surveys, parish baptismal
registers and regional historical monographs, this gazetteer establishes a
consistent spatial baseline for demographic disaggregation from the arrival of the
Portuguese at Calicut to the establishment of British territorial rule in Bengal.

The catalogued settlements reflect two and a half centuries of commercial contact
and urban nucleation across four macro-regions: the Konkan, Gujarat and Estado da
India littoral (562 settlements); the Malabar coast factories (263 settlements); the
Coromandel coast enclaves (341 settlements); and the Hugli-Bengal factories alongside
maritime Ceylon (314 settlements). While major fortified trading posts like Bombay
(542k peak), Calcutta (367k peak), Madras (347k peak) and Velha Goa (70k peak)
anchored global commercial flows, the demographic weight of early modern South Asia
resided within expansive indigenous artisan and market centres including Hampi
(233k peak), Murshidabad (136k), Ahmedabad (131k), Surat (122k), Gaur (114k) and
Vijayapura (93k).

Every catalogued entry conforms to geographic inclusion standards. Localities possess
documented WGS84 coordinates, historical toponyms cross-referenced against early
modern European and Asian cartography, and validated population benchmarks derived
from contemporary censuses and retrospective historical reconstructions. All 1.480
entries reconcile with the source ledger alongside 800 documented candidate
exclusions (primarily spatial consolidations within 3 km and non-residential
toponyms), documenting the spatial distribution of the 71M inhabitants of the
maritime domain at 1757AD.

# Coastal Enclaves and Settlement Systems

Early modern urban systems along the Indian Ocean seaboard reflected structural
interactions between European commercial institutions and indigenous urban
traditions [@Malekandathil2020Maritime; @Pearson1971Commerce]. Four primary
settlement types characterised the maritime urban landscape:

1. Fortified Naval Enclaves: Typified by Velha Goa, Diu, Daman, Bassein, Fort
Manuel in Cochin, Fort Geldria in Pulicat, Fort St George in Madras, Fort William in
Calcutta, and Fort d'Orléans in Chandernagore [@Ames2000Renascent; @Forrest1908Siege].
These settlements combined heavy stone curtain walls, bastions and artillery batteries
with European administrative quarters, garrisons, dockyards and cathedrals,
exercising sovereign jurisdiction over immediately adjacent districts
[@Chakrabarti2006Neither; @Abreu2020Health].

2. Riverine and Roadstead Factory Lodges: In major indigenous commercial ports such as
Surat, Bharuch, Masulipatnam and Hugli town, European trading nations maintained
unfortified commercial houses (*lodges*) under the authority of local governors,
coexisting within dense indigenous merchant quarters [@Kruijtzer2009Xenophobia;
@Arasaratnam1967Dutch]. These factories functioned as warehouses, residential
compounds and trading exchanges coordinating with native brokers (*dalals*) and
shroffs [@Pearson1971Commerce; @Clegg2017East].

3. Specialized Artisan and Weaver Hamlets: Distributed throughout coastal deltas
and river corridors, thousands of agricultural and manufacturing villages produced
export textiles under advance-contract systems (*dadni*). Settlements in the Cauvery,
Krishna-Godavari and lower Ganges deltas housed specialized castes of weavers,
bleachers and dyers who supplied cotton calicoes, muslins and chintz to European
purchasers [@Arasaratnam1967Dutch; @Subrahmanyam1989Coromandel].

4. Cinnamon and Spice Production Villages: Across maritime Ceylon and the Malabar
backwaters, rural settlements were organised around the compulsory harvesting of
cinnamon bark (*chalia* peelers under *rajakariya* service in Ceylon) and pepper
cultivation, integrating village agrarian structures with corporate export
monopolies [@WINTERBOTTOM2009Producing; @Lohuizen1961Dutch].

# Methodology and Source Ledger Reconciliation

Candidate localities in the INDUS source ledger were evaluated using published
gazetteers, archival surveys from the Portuguese Historical Archive (Arquivo
Historico Ultramarino), the Dutch National Archives (Nationaal Archief) and the
British Library Oriental and India Office Collections, alongside archaeological site
catalogues [@Ratcliff2025Monopolizi; @Embleton2023Names]. Inclusion requires:
- Precise geographic coordinates referenced to the WGS84 datum.
- Documented early modern historical occupation spanning 1498AD to 1757AD.
- Quantitative or narrative demographic evidence calibrated against contemporary
tax rolls, house counts or regional settlement densities.

# Macro-Regional Settlement Catalogues

## Konkan, Gujarat and Estado da India Littoral

The western maritime macro-region catalogues 562 settlements spanning Gujarat, the
Konkan coast and Goa [@Pearson1971Commerce; @Ames2000Renascent]. The leading urban
nucleus was Bombay (Mumbai), which expanded from 386k in 1550AD to a peak of 542k in
1650AD, retaining 359k in 1757AD as British company commercial dominance solidified.
Surat represented the premier commercial emporium of the Mughal Empire, peaking at
122k inhabitants with dense suburbs of weavers, shroffs and Armenian traders
[@Kruijtzer2009Xenophobia; @Aslanian2004Trade].

Ahmedabad (131k peak), Bharuch (37k peak) and Patan (46k peak) anchored textile and
indigo production in Gujarat, while Pune (92k peak) expanded as the political seat
of the Maratha Peshwas. The Portuguese capital at Velha Goa peaked at 70k residents,
supported by ecclesiastical palaces, the Royal Hospital and suburban parishes
across Salcette and Bardez [@Abreu2020Health; @Paiva2022Concord]. Fortified coastal
strongholds at Diu, Daman, Bassein and Chaul commanded transit dues across the Gulf
of Khambhat and Konkan waterways.

## Malabar Coast Factories

The Malabar coast catalogues 263 settlements along the southwest seaboard
[@Malekandathil2020Maritime; @degard2019Constructi]. Pre-colonial regional authority
centred on Hampi (Vijayanagara, 233k peak) in the interior plateau and the Sultanate
capital at Vijayapura (Bijapur, 93k peak). Along the immediate coastline, Calicut
(Kozhikode, 46k peak) functioned as the historic seat of the Zamorins, while Cochin
(Kochi, 37k peak) housed Portuguese and Dutch naval shipyards alongside Jewish and
Christian commercial communities [@degard2019Constructi].

Additional coastal factories and trading stations included Cannanore (Fort St
Angelo), Quilon (Kollam), French Mahé (founded 1721AD), Purakkad and
Thiruvananthapuram (42k peak), which expanded into the capital of the Travancore
Kingdom under Marthanda Varma [@Lohuizen1961Dutch].

## Coromandel Coast Enclaves

The Coromandel seaboard catalogues 341 settlements across Tamil Nadu and Andhra
Pradesh [@Arasaratnam1967Dutch; @Subrahmanyam1989Coromandel]. Madras (Chennai)
constituted the largest company metropolis, growing from an unpopulated sandy spit
in 1639AD to 347k residents by 1757AD, organised into segregated White and Black
Towns [@Chakrabarti2006Neither; @Clegg2017East]. Traditional dynastic and religious
centres retained large populations: Thanjavur (75k peak), Madurai (70k peak),
Tiruchirappalli (56k peak) and Kanchipuram (56k peak).

Commercial enclaves included Dutch Fort Geldria in Pulicat, Dutch Nagapattinam (32k
peak), French Pondicherry (Puducherry, 42k peak), Danish Tranquebar (Tharangambadi)
and the Sultanate emporium of Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam, 47k peak)
[@Forrest1908Siege; @Subrahmanyam1989Coromandel; @Kruijtzer2009Xenophobia]. Further
south in the Gulf of Mannar, sacred chank and pearl fisheries supported maritime
settlements from Tuticorin to Rameswaram [@Hornell1914Sacred].

## Hugli-Bengal Factories and Maritime Ceylon

The eastern macro-region catalogues 314 settlements across the lower Bengal delta
and the island of Ceylon [@Robins2012Corporatio; @WINTERBOTTOM2009Producing].
Calcutta (Kolkata) expanded rapidly from three agricultural villages in 1690AD to
reach 367k inhabitants by 1757AD, eclipsing the historic Sultanate capital of Gaur
(114k peak) and the Nawabi capital of Murshidabad (136k peak).

Along the Hugli River, European competitors clustered within short distances: Dutch
Chinsurah, French Chandernagore, Danish Serampore and Portuguese Hugli. In maritime
Ceylon, Colombo (56k peak) anchored Dutch cinnamon collection, flanked by the
fortified naval harbor at Galle, Jaffna, Trincomalee and coastal peelers' villages
[@Parthesius2010Dutch; @WINTERBOTTOM2009Producing].

# Source Ledger Audit and Excluded Candidates

The INDUS source ledger records 2.280 candidates across the maritime domain. Of
these, 1.480 were included as catalogued settlements, while 800 entries were
excluded. Exclusions conform to systematic criteria:
1. Spatial deduplication (duplicate aliases): satellite survey coordinates and
suburban hamlets situated within 3 km of a primary nucleated settlement were
consolidated into the canonical record to prevent artificial clustering.
2. Non-residential toponyms: isolated lighthouses, offshore reefs, navigation
shoals and administrative divisions lacking permanent habitation were removed.

Table \ref{tab:excluded} documents the leading 25 excluded candidates alongside
their canonical primary settlement and justification.

# Limitations and Preservation Biases

Historical demographic analysis of early modern Indian coastal settlements faces
specific taphonomic and documentary constraints:
1. Asymmetric Record Preservation: While European company archives document factory
personnel and trade values in detail, indigenous census data outside formal company
boundaries remain fragmentary [@Ratcliff2025Monopolizi; @Robins2012Corporatio].
2. Suburban and Transient Under-Enumeration: High seasonal mobility among weavers,
cart drivers and sailors produced substantial population turnover that was rarely
captured in static municipal rolls [@Chakrabarti2006Neither; @Rossum2019Labouring].
3. Fluvial and Geomorphological Change: Active siltation and channel migration along
the Hugli and deltaic rivers buried early modern wharf structures and shifted port
approaches over time [@Malekandathil2020Maritime].

Despite these constraints, reconciling 1.480 catalogued localities provides a
robust quantitative framework for early modern South Asian demographic history.
